blocks.x: I'll make a note on here we're interviewing Dr. Edmond Sushan up at his office at 2400 Canal. This is Bill Russell interviewing and the date is February the 17th, 1962. Do you mind giving your full name and if you don't mind your birth date and all?

Okay, Bill. It's October the 25th, 1897. My name is Dr. Edmond Sushan II. No middle name? No middle name. I am named for my grandfather who was Edmond Sushan I. My father was marrying Sim Sushan so I couldn't be junior. I was born in the front room on St. Charles and First Street and my grandfather delivered me.
Oh, he did? Yeah.
And if I remember the gory details, I weighed nine pounds or something. What was the date? October the 25th, 97. 97, alright.
Let's see. How far back can you remember?

I believe Bill, I tried to set it in an article I wrote recently about Oliver and they clipped out a great deal of the memories that made me verify that. I remember the morning or night that my sister was born.
She was four years old.

I was four years older than her. And I remember the night she was born distinctly because they had two bedrooms, the front one and the second one. And I was put in the second bedroom and they had mosquito bars and they pinned a sheet around it. And I saw an old aunt that used to be in the family who always was present at births, deaths, and marriages. And she was there that night. And that was a clear, distinct memory. I still remember it now.
That's pretty good. I used to think I could remember back three years, when I was three once, my brother had an operation.
You do remember that?
Now I don't know if I just remember the memory of that or if I actually remember the time. The, going through the door and which room it was in.

I was trying to check on that since you asked me for this interview. By measuring on the front picket fence. I remember resting my chin on the fence. I was just that high. And I must have been no more than four or five at that time.

I had an uncle, which is remarkable. He went to, made a visit to Pittsburgh when he was between two, wasn't even three, two years old. And years later, he never went back, but he could draw a plan of the yard where he played.
I'll be here.
And I think he really proved it.
Well, I think they do.
I think they do.

Although the Catholic faith regards the age of reason at age seven, the memory dates way before that. That's been proven. How far back, I don't know. I'll tell you another thing that I remember so distinctly, and I was age four then. The people next door were the Stevens, Harry Stevens, that had this, what do you call it, clothing store, Stevens on Canal Street. Oh, yeah. Next to us, and in the back of our yard, they had their stable. And there was a beautiful stallion that they had, one of them used to drive. And the thing was frightened by an automobile, and it went over the picket fence and was impaled on there. And I remember them taking me away because they were going to shoot the horse. Now, those are distinct memories that are big milestones. So when I try to go back, it means that I am thinking pretty well straight at that time. Now, you asked me the other day about when my first remembrance of anything connected with jazz, I'd say music, if you will. Yeah, just music. We had a cook, two of them in fact, that followed each other, Amotin and Adele. Well, Amotin was really the best of the two, but both of them, you want to check it? No, I'm sorry.
I looked down a few minutes.

Don't worry. Both of them were singers, and they both had very fine contralto voices. And it amazed me because they were singing a type of music I'd never heard before. It was definitely the type of stuff Mahalia Jackson and them do it. They were the same type of hymns, not as well done, of course. But they had a quiver in the way they would duck certain notes and flatten them that was amazing to me. It used to fascinate me. I'd be in the yard playing and I could hear them singing. They were watching me play that. And then the memory that I have of actually being exposed to the music was when Amotin, and as I said, I wondered how the grapevine got around that there was going to be a funeral. But there was a cemetery on Washington Avenue, maybe about eight, ten blocks from our house. Still one there.
Yes.

And the parades, which started usually from the Bulls, that's my memory that they started there. They would always pass Terrell's Grocery on First Street, which was two or three blocks back of our house on First. And my cook always took me there to see the funerals. And we'd second line, I'd walk right along with the gang. And that is my first exposure. It was confusing to me, but it was thrilling. I enjoyed it. Maybe it was because the uniforms were gaudy. But at the time, I felt very much drawn to this youngster who was playing the cornet at the time. It was Joe Oliver. Joe Oliver. Yeah. And he worked in the neighborhood. My memory is that he was somebody's yard man between camp and magazine in that neighborhood, on First or Third. I can't pin it down any closer than that.

I think it was on Second. At least two or three people told me, Second and Magazine. And I took pictures of all four corners on there. I once took a picture of what I thought would be the building and showed it to Bunk. Bunk said, that's not it. Bunk used to go there and steal music from him, they said.
He did, yeah.
So Bunk was dead before I took the other three corners, but Louie Kepard, who I think would, who worked with Oliver at that same period. Uh-huh.

Well, let me tell you another memory I have of Joe Oliver that was funny. Although he was only 16 or something like that at the time, if my memory serves me right. He was, I see, much older to a kid who was four years old, five years old. And I was struck by what beautiful white teeth he had. And he always chewed a hunk of tar. You know that black stuff? Oh, yeah. They always chewed that.
I know those people did that.
Always chewed that.
Now, uh- What kind of music did you have in your home? Any of your-

Well, a mother played piano a little bit. One day she took me down in the living room and played a waltz and then she played a mazurka. And she said, this is the sum total of $5,000 of lessons. Now then my dad, who was a very busy surgeon, he told me that he played French horn in a college band at Spring Hill. And he also learned how to fool with the guitar a little bit in college, just to sing a few little ditties and things like that. But that's as far as it went. Now next door at my grandfather's place, they had everything. They had a piano, one of these kind you roll up to the-
Yeah, I've seen it.

Put it with the fingers in it. And they had all kinds of records. They didn't simply lean to the classics. They also included ragtime. And they had the face phonograph, the little cylinder ones that I just wish to the Lord I had now. I can remember some of the songs they sang. And one of them was, The Iceman is a nice man, but just one thing is sure. There's something in his business that affects his temperature. Oh, love is such a funny thing, just a fondle once or twice. But all you get from the Iceman is ice, ice, ice. And it terminated by saying, sung by Billy Jones and Ada Murray. Oh, yeah. And they had all kinds of those things. Yeah, Columbia, I think, had that. Then he had a great big music box with flat cylinders with holes in them. The Kim disc. Discs, that's right. And those were, they really had a great deal of that around the house.
I like that song on there.

My grandmother is actually the one who got me interested in music. She used to play piano a little bit and she'd get songs and knew enough about them. I remember probably the first two that she tried to teach me was one of them. Oh, my baby, my curly-headed baby, we'll sit beneath the sky and sing a song to the moon. That was one of them. And the other one was, I forget. But then I had an aunt that made a trip to Hawaii and brought back the first ukulele that I ever saw in my life. She brought it to me. And I fiddled with it a little bit. Regular four string like the modern one? Four string. Smaller to me. Smaller. Even as a child, when things usually look large, it looked smaller to me then. But they had a book of instructions and I couldn't get a thing out of it. Now, around, when I was around eight or nine, maybe ten even, my mother and father decided that I should take music and I picked the guitar. And they hired a very sweet lady who was the sister of a doctor, Miss Caznavet. She was very lovely and she really knew how to play a guitar. But classics, you know, Fandango and all that stuff. And she began with Solfegeo and all that business. Well, I lasted exactly three lessons and they told me that I was hopeless. Nothing pleased me more than twenty years later to be invited to a recital. Bernie Shields and I were the featured artists and she was on the front row. But then, Bill, the guitar got put aside. Yeah. And it just molded in the case. Until some people living two doors from us. There was our house, no, first my grandfather's, then my house, then the Stevens, and the next door was the Victor Greenmire family. And they decided to have dancing lessons. And I remember I had a damn good lambing because I wouldn't go. I had to get all dressed up and polished and I didn't want to go where there was girls anyhow. But when I got there, there was a little old dried up lady. She must have been seventy then and she lived to be ninety and still worked professionally playing ragtime on the piano. All we did was a two step then. And I remember. How old were you then? I must have been about eight and nine. At most ten. And then when the dancing school got going real good, they used to have three pieces. A piano, a guitar, and a bass. Real ragtime. And they switched from this white woman to three Negroes. Well, nobody beat me after that. I used to hang around the band and watch the guitar play. And that's when I began going home fooling around with it. Then the next move that made me get more deeply involved in it, I used to go across to past Christiane to visit the George W. Clays. And they were first at Bay St. Louis and then past Christiane. And I brought my guitar along with me and one of their boys played a mandolin and piano, younger than I was. And I discovered, they used to have bands play, oh maybe once a month for big dances over there. And I asked the guitar player if I could come to his place to get lessons. And he charged me twenty-five cents an hour. I had to walk about fifteen blocks both ways. It was a little shack way in the back. And the family was just up in arms that I was doing such a thing. But he'd get a mandolin and I'd get a guitar and he'd just sit me down and begin playing. Now that band was, I don't remember the name of his last name. The leader was their chauffeur. His name was Armand, A-R-M-A-N-D. Not P-R-R-O-N. But Armand was his first name. And they had a full eight or nine piece band which even back, well you add from age ten that would make it what about, Nineteen seven, nineteen seven, nineteen eight. They had two saxes in the band. And even that, yes sir, even that early. They were competing with Buddy Petit's band at the same time. Buddy Petit was as we know in Covington, Mandeville, Bita Springs in that area. But once in a while they'd bring him in to play and there would be a competition between these two bands. And that's why I heard Buddy Petit a great deal. I was amazed by his neck would swell out so far. Did anybody else tell you that about his playing?
I'm not sure.

When he blew he evidently either had, it was a bad embouchure or he was instructed wrong. But his neck would swell way out and one side of his face would puff way out. Now it may have helped him sustain the note, you know, to have all that extra air there. But he looked funny as a dickens.
Well, Louis Armstrong's neck comes out so far and George Brunus' whole face comes out.
And what's the matter with big Jim Robinson? Yeah, he comes out. He's got two pouches on the side of his face that come out.
I think George's face swells out more as the whole face in there. And Louis' neck comes out. Other people's neck, too, have seen it.

Well, he did that. Then we had a little, on the end of the wharf at Past Christiana, there used to be a four-piece string band, sort of a spasm band, four little colored boys. For two dollars they'd play the whole evening. And I mean they played practically with no rest period. I mean we'd start at seven o'clock and the whole thing was over at ten. Let's turn it off. My secretary's coming, just for a minute.
We were talking about the little band over there.

Yeah. There was a homemade guitar, a homemade bass, a harmonica, and a comb. And they did a great deal of singing and hand clapping, too. And I have a distinct memory of one song there that I have threatened to record, because it was so repetitious. I only remember one voice. It was called, Yonder Come the Hoodoo Conducta Man. It went something like this. When you see me coming, my grip sack in my hand, then you'll know you saying, Yonder Come the Hoodoo Conducta Man. And that went on and on and on. They may have had one, two voices, but I don't remember them at all.
Well, to get back to this other band, this seven or eight piece band, were they all local fellows there, do you think?

Oh, yes, all out of past Christian. You're pretty sure they didn't come from here and go over there? No, no, no, no, no. They were local. And the only time they brought an imported band was with Buddy Petit's.
How did it compare with the New Orleans style? Was there much difference, do you think?

Very similar, but there was a difference. And I think that without analyzing it at that time, I noticed there was a difference to my ear. I think it was due to the saxophones, and I didn't like them worth a damn.
I never did either myself.

Then along the line here, I would say around, I must have been no older than 12, maybe 11. We suddenly discovered there were other boys that were playing. We never had gotten together. Everybody was afraid to come out, afraid to show how little they knew. But finally, I went at an invitation to Bob and Harry Reynolds. They lived on Britannia Street, the corner of Marengo on the Uptown Woods Corner. And they asked me to bring my guitar. Well, I hid it in the bushes, and then I went on in and I listened to the two brothers, a guitar and mandolin. And I listened to them play, and I said to myself, they're not a damn bit better than I am. So then I went out and got my guitar and brought it out of the bushes and brought it in. Well then gradually, every Sunday, we'd meet over at their house about 1 o'clock, and we'd play straight through. We'd all get down to our BVDs, as hot as the hinges. And all of us stuck in this one upstairs bedroom. It was a big two-story house. Then around 5.30 in the evening, Mrs. Reynolds and Mr. Reynolds would have us all down to supper. And I remember it was the first time I'd ever heard Grace sit at meals. And there was a big tall, high muck-a-muck in the Methodist face. And he had whiskers, and he looked just like a bishop himself. But anyway, they put up with our music. In spite of it being jazz, in spite of his being very holy, none of us were drinking at the time. You see, we were kids there then, and they were encouraging it. Well, it finally wound up we had two guitars, a mandolin, a banjo, two violins, and no bass fiddle. And if I can run over in the names a little bit, it'll help me. I forgot a ukulele. There was Midget Harrison, Hilton Harrison, who was a classic violinist, and who gave recitals. His mother was a classic teacher. And boy, I have heard Joe Venuti, and I've heard the records of Eddie South, and what's the name of this? The Feli in France? Grappoli, Stephen Grappoli. And of course my enthusiasm to them, both as being a partner and marking a milestone, maybe I'm warped in his favor, but that guy could really tear a fiddle to pieces. Then we had a second violinist who was also a classic violinist, but who played an entirely different style, and he was a good foil for the other one. His name was Roland Rorschach. We called him Rex. He was a Spanish fellow, very Mexican-looking. And then Bernie Shields played a banjo, sometimes a mandolin. Then Bob and Harry Reynolds, and Harry was the mandolin, Bob the guitar. I was another guitar. And then Charlie Hardy came in with the ukulele. And then we had others that joined us at odd intervals. There was Bill Gibbons who played a guitar mandolin. It's the only one I've ever seen like it. It was a guitar about the size of a ukulele. But it had six double strings, you see, but it had a not too unpleasant tone, but it didn't add anything to the group, you see. No. Because he didn't play cording, he actually picked a melody on the thing.
How old were you then?

Oh, I would say around 11, 12 years old. That's all. Maybe 14 years, I don't know you. Not that old. No, we didn't ever leave that house for three years. We practiced until we were about 14. Then we began going out. Now there were a lot of older men in the crowd, and I wouldn't say older. Oh yeah, I know. Maybe 15, 16, they were old compared to us. But then when I got to be about 14, then we actually ventured out and began playing on Sunday night after we'd practiced all afternoon at the Reynolds' we'd go to some girl's house, and they'd give you cokes and sandwiches and spend the whole evening. Then the thing got to be very regular, either Saturday or Sunday or both, where nobody was invited to these parties unless they could sing or play. And that's how I ran into my wife. She was a classical piano teacher, but she also played a very good jazz ragtime piano, if you will. They were already getting away from the ragtime, although I remember many of the pieces that she had was entertainers rag, the maple leaf and all those. Others were beginning to come in, and the style of playing was changing then. I don't think we ever played what really would be called ragtime. It was always. And the thing that made us compete and improve was we had a group opposite to us. There was a boy who lived right across from the Reynolds. Why the Reynolds has never invited him over, I'll never understand, because he was a better musician than any of us, and that was Bill Clappinger. He was an orphan, and he would sit alone on his porch and practice hour after hour, and those Reynolds never invited him over. Now he became one of a group that was a very fine bunch of musicians. They all knew cording and arrangements and stuff much better than we did. They would call themselves the Invincibles, and they were really a hot competition with us. They had some fine musicians in there.
Were the winds in there or just strings?

All strings, yes. All strings. I was going to tell you. Red Mackey was on bass and banjo. Frank Mackey is his name, they called him Red. Then Rene Jelpe was on banjo. They had Eblen Rau on violin, Roletishner on guitar, Monk Smith, did I mention him? No. Monk Smith on guitar and Uke. And they had about seven or eight in the crowd. But I realize now, looking back, that they really were much better than we were. But we had the pep and the zip, and we'd work up some kind of little singing things with it. Incidentally, Bill, when you said people thought I couldn't sing, they never would let me sing. They thought I sang so loud that they wouldn't let me sing. Then we had a group that sang that let me contribute that, but not otherwise. And so that's the group, the Invincibles, that became eventually the Owls. Monk Smith took up clarinet and saxophone, and he also played his guitar with the band, but with a capadastro, just like I did. And Rene Jelpe continued on his banjo. Benji White was one of their, he became a sax and clarinet player. Red Mackey switched to piano and bass after they became the Owls. And that's about all of that group that really went into the Owls. But the minute they started with wind instruments, they broke up right now.
Did you ever have any more lessons there during that period?

No, no. Outside of, well, up at the Tulane Gym when I began hearing the real good bands, I would stick on Johnny St. Cyr's neck a whole evening. I never left him, and he would always show me little things to do. There's no formal lessons there. No. Incidentally, we're still friends, Bill. I get a letter from him at least once a month. He wired me and wrote me when his wife died recently, and he's just had a cataract operation. He said he had that.
I didn't know he had that.
I think he just did.
Some friends said, well, you're going to have it too late, maybe not save it.

Well, the last news I got was about two weeks ago from a fellow by the name of, that was in here recently. Slingsby. Slingsby, who wrote me, I have a letter from him just the other day, saying that Johnny was going into the hospital. I haven't heard how it came out.
He's going to put it off and...

Now, he's going to send us his guitar for the museum. He's promised me that, but he won't send it because it's broken. I said, I don't give a damn. Send it. I'll fix it. I'll get Bill to fix it for me.
He'll sting it up somewhere.
I'll get it. So, anyway, when we began...
I don't want to interrupt you, but I wonder how you have that very oldest train of memory going. What about Mardi Gras parades when you were a kid?
They all passed right in front of my house.
What kind of bands did they have?
I remember Jack Lane's on Mardi Gras day. I don't remember it as Jack Lane's, but I remember it was... How many bands did they have?
It would be just one good jazz band?
That's all I remember. It's one fine jazz band which followed the king or was preceding the king.
There wouldn't be one between each float or anything.

There was, but there were not as many as there were today. And there was none of these formations of marching high school girls and boys. The only time they used what they called the militia then was on the day before Mardi Gras, which has been dispensed with.
I remember when Rex had come in.

They came in on the river front. There was a substitute king, one float was a substitute king. And they came down, steamed down the river, and then they were met by the militia. Jack played in that outfit too, but I don't remember him like I do in front of my house, because many times they stopped directly in front of my house and people would dance in the streets. Not like today. Everybody was joining in on the thing.
How old would you be that you remember those things?
At least I remember it couldn't be more than six or seven. It couldn't possibly be more than that.
And how late did that last? I lost track.

I lost track. The minute I started getting a little bit older, the intense interest, when the minute I started going to Tulane, I began to have to study a little bit, and then the music began falling in the background, although we did play once in a while. Now then we began getting our music, as I say through the regular bands. And Oliver, comparatively late, because he began playing up at the gym. I remember I was going up to those gym dances on Saturday night before I was even in Tulane. A dollar a couple. Oh yes, a subscription dance. And all you got was ice water in the band and a hell of a good floor and you'd dance all evening. But before that Oliver period, we used to have fraternity dances. OBD was a high school fraternity. DTO was another one. And they always had dancers and bands. And I remember the bands that they hired at the time, one of them was McCollum's. Whenever they were hired McCollum's band, it was because they couldn't afford a good band. He charged less than the others. And boy, he blew more bad notes than you ever imagined. And he had a bad embouchure because I remember he had a big white button sticking out on his lip that was just like a headlight on him. He always had pretty good men. And one of the men that played with him before the formation of Pierron's band was Louis Warnicke. I have a picture of Louis with McCollum's. I think you gave me a copy of that.
Yeah.

But anyway, another band that they only used when they had to was Louis Armstrong's band. He played, you know, he wasn't the leader. But he blew so damn loud that you had to have a hall as big as the auditorium to take him. And I'm not so sure he was always on the button with his notes either. He only became good, really good, when he began playing on the Steamer. He was the president. No, what is it? The Sidney or Capitola. Yeah, yeah, yeah. The bands that we danced by, the Silverleaf, Mapleleaf, Goldleaf, Tuxedo, as I said, McCollum's. And then a great deal, as we grew a little bit older into the town when we began going out with the debutants, then we began going to Antoine's, you know, it's La Louisiane, which is now, was occupied, the area which is presently occupied by the Playbar Club and Moran's Restaurant. Now, that whole thing was La Louisiane, and their band, the house band there, was Robichaud.
And you mentioned the other day you'd like to tell us something about that.

Now, Robichaud, to me, he was one of the most polished gentlemen that I ever knew. He was soft-spoken, very well educated, and as we all know, he was a left-hand violinist. And strictly readers, every one of them in the band, they had their arrangements up in front of them. But he always had one or two hot takeoff men in the band. He may have a nucleus of six, but he'd have either a good trumpet or a good takeoff clarinet. I'm very certain that I've often heard Perez play in that group there. Once in a while, they would hire him, especially when it was a big dance, and Lorenzo Teo Jr. played once in a while with him too. Who the rest of the band was, I don't know. I knew them at the time, because I always was hanging around the bandstand. But they played strictly, more strictly arranged than Piran did.
What type of music otherwise, I mean, in the way of waltzes or...
They had a waltz, they had a waltz about every third or fourth dance then. And nobody but the chaperones would dance then.
Really? Yeah.

Once, one or fewer, the younger people would. But the only dance that they had then at the time was the two-step, but that became extremely intricate. The steps had developed along with that. And it was not because the, what do you call them, the castles came. Irene Castle and Osborne came and played at the St. Charles. Had a very fine place upstairs. Piran was a band, and they danced, the castles danced to them. But that didn't influence the dancing that we did. We were moving along. Who brought it in, I don't know, but it became very intricate steps. A great deal of turning and twisting and side steps and all that would be very difficult for the kids, even though they are good dancers today. It would be very difficult for them to do that. And, let's see, can you stop it a minute? It looks like you're running out. Yeah. You got enough room? The dancing today is, if you'll notice, is with the people with their bodies apart, not touching. But on the contrary, when we were dancing, you had direct body contact with a grip all the way around the girl. And not for a sexual reason, although there were some that would get over in the corner and roll it, you know. But what they did was to, those steps had to be perfect between the couples or it wouldn't go. And, as I say, very rapid, intricate changes of steps. It became first the two steps, then the one step. But we didn't do the Charleston and those as a group very much. A few people did it for frills and that's about all.
Yeah.
They did have a dancing school. Mm-hm.
You mentioned Mrs. Lewis's dancing school.

Well, actually, it was a place that everybody went. There were some that signed up to go to these dances over a period, but you could get in for a dollar on a Saturday night. It was actually a dance more than it was a dancing school. And at that time, a lot of the boys and girls would just go there because there was no dance going on, no script dance up at Tulane. And instantly, I want to come back to Tulane again. I remember what the Oliver Band was paid. They were paid $28 for seven men, but you had to guarantee them four quarts, four fifths. Four quarts, fifths weren't in existence then, of whiskey, which cost us 50 or 60 cents a quart. And guess what it was? Twenty-year-old, old Taylor, old granddad, and all the things that we'd pay through the nose. The old bottles and all? Oh, yes. Oh, yes. And little by little, I don't ever remember seeing any of them taking a drink, but boy, they really knocked down on those, yeah. And a thing that's interesting, too, the music got hot like it would you'd expect because little that I know about it, everybody thinks they're playing well and they're playing loud when they have a few drinks. But as the evening wore on, it got more and more blue as they leaned down in their chair and just took it as easy as they could. And Johnny has told you, I'm sure if you've interviewed him, about this little drummer. I believe his name was Zeno.
Is that his name? One time it was a happy bowl.

Well, that's the guy that used to sing the dirty songs. And they would all be hanging around his chair there because, as you know, how many of these songs that have perfectly respectable words and all, but one of them was Take Your Hand Out of Katie's Ass. That was one of them. And, oh, Mama's Baby Boy had foul words to that thing.
Yeah, all of them.
Camellia Gaspargoo.
Yeah.

That's one they clipped out for me on Golden Crest. And, well, even, I'm trying to think of some of the others that they used to sing. They were all foul. But anyway, many times, our group of six and seven-eighths wouldn't dance at all. Most of us would just hang around the band and watch and listen. We never did come anywhere near to what they were doing, but at least we'd learn the tunes and try to do it a little bit the way they did. And I remember Oliver impressing me even more up there because I think, to me, that was when he was at his peak. But he had to change his style a little bit from what I'd heard him playing down at Big 25, somewhere in the interim there. And that was rough stuff. And they began polishing it up when they went to the gym to adapt themselves to the dancers. They couldn't dance to the kind of music, although they liked the sound of it, and they realized it. And I come back to this point that I made several times. I think I've referred to it in an article that they accidentally, upon purpose, they clipped out, was the fact that high society was used not as a dance tune when they'd say, when you'd have a party and it was for a plate lunch or supper around 11.30. They'd get the couples together by playing a march. And it was an interminable march. They'd play that intro. That went on and on. And so slow, it was like a dirge march almost. Nobody could dance to high society. Then when the people began insisting on it being played, they stepped the tempo up. But that is not the original way they played it. They played a very slow tempo.
You know, some of the colored dances they'd used is Gettysburg, the 6-8 to start with, sort of the pistachio. Yes, that's exactly it.
That's exactly it.
And they used high society...

Exactly the same way. The personnel of the band was something that was interesting, too. I remember Ori playing with them. I remember Johnny Dodds. I don't remember Baby Dodds playing with them. If he did, I don't remember it. Bob Foster played with them sometimes. And then what's this other bass down here? It was either of those two were always in demand. Ed Garland. Ed Garland. Garland, but there was still another one. I don't remember. There's so many of them around here. I remember something that none of the records ever... Nothing that Oliver ever did on any of the records approached his real peak at the time. He could take one note and sustain that through a whole damn chorus of the band doing the changes behind it. Just one. He'd just hold it just as clean and pure as you ever heard.
I never heard that on a record. No.

And as I say, hearing him again in Chicago, he had completely changed his style. He was trying to play like a white band. They were even adding instruments, a couple of saxes and all. They had lost it. And people went nuts about it. It's the closest thing to an example of it that they had. But I would say the Ory group out on the West Coast when they had... Who was the little trumpet player?
Mud Carey.
Mud Carey. And was it Joe Darnsberg? Yeah, Joe Darnsberg. Joe Darnsberg. And Bud Scott.
Ram Hall and Bud Scott.

That is the closest thing to the old type of music that Bud... That Oliver played in those days. Yes, yes. They were dressed up and they were big shots and all that. And the attitude was very nice. I mean, the one that was pretty much of a... felt his oats very much was Baby Todd's when he was in Chicago. But Oliver was just as cordial and nice as he could be. Incidentally, from a doctor's standpoint, I am convinced that he had diabetes. Yeah, you told me that, Mark. Because the fact that he would drink these buckets of sugar water he had next to the band. He'd just sop that up. It's a craving for sweets.
Yeah.
And he was a terrible eater, as the story goes.
Oh, yeah. He really must have been. He wouldn't talk that way.

I remember Oliver when people wouldn't have remembered him. I remember him with cut shoes. They'd buy a $25 pair of floor charms and cut with a brand new knife there with a knife. They'd cut these new shoes so their feet wouldn't hurt them.
Oh, little slits in the side?

Yeah. Oh, like just up and down, straight across. They could just open up like that. I also remember him wearing a red undershirt and suspenders. And he'd cock that derby hat over that bad eye. And I don't know who else has told you this, but we never knew him as Joe Oliver. We called him Monocle. When he blew that bad eye, which was a white eye, he sustained a traumatic cataract in a fight, and that eye was perfectly white. And when he blew that high note, that one eye would, even though he closed the other one, that one eye would stick out just like, it looked like a monocle sticking out there. And it was not done in derision. The name was never done with anything but great affection to him. And he knew his name that way. Now, hold it off a minute, and let's see what else we can dig up, because you start running.
It really is.
You asked me a little bit, to elucidate about the guitar players. Yeah, guitar. Well, we were...
Or a banjo. Also, when that came in,

you know, those different things. Well, I want to say just this, that I remember very few banjos in the band until much, much later. Very few. In fact, I don't remember any in Oliver's band until Johnny St. Cyr began pulling out that homemade six-string guitar of his. And I want to say this, too, that Johnny St. Cyr used a cappodastro. And he made his out of a lead pencil that he put across the bridge with string that he tied on. And he had to have two guitars. If they're playing an F or a natural key, he'd pick up the one that didn't have a cappodastro. And whenever he played the E-flat, A-flat, or B-flat, he'd use the other one. And now, Johnny was more accustomed to using a heavy pick when he played with the band and how those strings withstood that onslaught because I think you're familiar with the story that not only I but others have told you. The pick that he had, that he played with, was made from a bone toothbrush that he cut to about two inches. He still uses that. And then he filed it down to a very fine feather edge. But most of the guitar players that I heard were all pickers, thumb and forefingers. And there wasn't a place you could go. They were all over the place.
How many fingers did they use, actually?
They'd rest their little finger on the guitar and the motion would be with these two fingers. Seldom, if ever, the third finger.
Just the index finger and the thumb.

Index and thumb, yeah. Now, we used to hear them in Amit. That's the place where McKay had a, his folks had a plantation up there. And they were still all over the place. They were getting few, but many of them we heard were there.
The classical Segovia style uses the thumb and three more fingers in the high string. But you all didn't do that.
Well, what ruined my playing was those three lessons I had with that woman.
Yeah.
I was supposed to use all five of them.
Yeah, that's complicated.

And it just messed me up. I couldn't get that stroke. Now, Thompson McKay, there were two brothers, Percy and Thompson. Percy is one of the vice presidents of the Whitney Bank. Thompson's a consulting engineer in Dallas for one of the very big engineering firms. He was better than Percy and he had that Negro style down pat. He played just exactly like they did in the cornfield plantation stuff. Now, the best guitarist that I ever heard any place, and I don't think there'll ever be one before or after, no matter how much that technique is brilliant for single string stuff, Snooze of Quinn will never be ever touched by anybody. Now, he played with an unamplified guitar except for the last five years of his life. And that was the most discreet amplification I've ever heard. You couldn't tell it was amplified at all, except that everybody in the room could hear it. And he had a vibrato that he used with his foot on this thing that was terrific, too. Yeah. That was a sustained note. But he'd have the whole thing, the lead, the treble, the lead, the accompaniment, and the bass going at one time.
You can hear that on those records that Johnny had him to record. Yes, indeed. Did he do much better than that? Those are plenty good.
Well, yes, he did much better than that.
Of course, he was sick in the hospital and all that. I wondered if he did.
Now, another thing, too, that not much is mentioned about Snooze that could sing to beat hell. And he was a marvelous violin player. Did you know that, too, Johnny?
Somebody told me that once, but I never did.

He did this old stunt that Joe Venuti does. He loosened the bow until the horsehair was very loose. And then he'd put it upside down over the thing. And he'd play four chord tunes on the thing, which was fabulous. But any place that Snooze would win, nobody would play there. Everybody would quit and just go around. Even up at the Tulane gym, if you brought it up there, all of them would quit and listen to him. But he didn't care to practice. He practiced maybe six or eight hours, but never formally. He'd practice alone for himself.
He didn't care. Did you ever play in any bands as much around here?
I know he did some, but I never heard of anything special. and things like that.
Things like that as well. No good bands.
Oh, the owls. He played with them for a while. I remember him playing out at Suburban Gardens with the owls.
Regular longer engagement.

Yes, a regular set thing. And he was terrific. They gave him stuff on the violin, breaks to do on that, and featured his singing and everything else. That's when they had very much larger group. They grew up to about a ten-piece band. The other guitarists around New Orleans proper were none that I know of except the McKay brothers, which were both white, and then all the Negro bands. And they all, as I say, I don't remember a banjo until much later when Johnny St. Cyr began using that six-string. Now, the... And they didn't use a piano if the guitar was there, and vice versa. They didn't use a guitar if the piano was there. Very seldom you'd have them both. And at the Tulane Gym, they never had any piano. Now, coming back to the Pierron band, I made a mistake in a statement I made a long time ago, and that was corrected by Mrs. Pierron. Steve Lewis, who played with Pierron, never did play with Oliver, although even Pierron led Oliver's band for many years on the violin up at the gym and all around town. And they used to practice music in his little barber shop, which was not far away from Big 25. Now, Pierron's band were also readers, and they used arrangements, but they did a great deal of takeoff. And the best one, of course, was Lorenzo Teo. I enjoyed Cottrell Sr. on drums very much. He was a big, tall, very black, but very well-chiseled features, and he had white, white hair, and he was a good dresser. But he had an extraordinary characteristic. His eyebrows would go up with every beat of the drum. He'd just look up. He'd move. His whole scalp would go up with every beat. On the offbeat, too. Always. Really? Yeah. Now, Pierron had a banjo with him as a rule, which was either, what's his name the trumpet players?
Charlie Bokaj.
Charlie Bokaj, what's the name of this other little short fellow?
Oh, Simon. Not Simon. John Marrero.
Marrero. Marrero.
He was with Celestan, though.
Wait. I have his picture, and I'm going to pull that out for you later on. No, wait a minute.
No, it wouldn't be Marrero. Anyway, I think it's on the picture.
I have it on one.
We have some of those pictures, too. Yeah, there's two different. That's right. I think it was John Marrero was with him, too.

Now, one of the things that was interesting to me is that even though Pierron was a dance orchestra, society dance orchestra, they loved to feature the tuba. And I don't remember very many tubas ever seeing a tuba with Oliver's band. It was always a string bass down there. I think it was because they need that slapping rhythm when they didn't have the piano. They needed that.
Most of the old timers say that the tuba was a little bit heavy. I mean, didn't have quite...
Did you ever see Chink Martin, age 74, walking along the street a mile a minute ahead of everybody else with a tuba under one arm and a bass fiddle under the other? That's a sight.
I've heard Chink, of course, play, remember those records that he made for Tulane one time.
Of course, he was at the end of his rope that night. He didn't care much, but he still enjoys his music. I'll click it a minute so we can come back to something else. There we will.
You're asking about the difference between banjo and guitar, which you really prefer and which most of the musicians here prefer. Why did the style change from one to the other?

Well, I personally rather play a banjo with a band. I think it kicks it along much better and they can't turn that damn microphone off like they do when I play a guitar. They can't hear me a damn bit and they're forced to hear me with a banjo. But personally, not only about myself, I think a banjo does kick a band along.
In the real old days, say back in the 1910 period, could you really hear that guitar? Because half the time you can't hear it.

You could if you were up close to the band, but I mean, having no microphones or anything like that, it just, I think it was for the band itself, the solid cording and the solid rhythm that they used, it helped the band itself more than it did the dancers. I think, of course, that the pieces like the blues had no business to be played on the banjo at all. Now, one of the things that I was going to completely overlook was the fact that we danced by Brown's band many times. Oh, yeah. And I followed, I used to go to the prize fights, I was quite a fan even as a kid, and that's why I was fortunate enough to hear both Happy Shilling and Brown's band and the third one, what's his name, Johnny Fisher.
I've been asking about Fisher's band.

Because they overlap. Fisher was in Shilling's band and then they'd want to get another pickup band, they'd call it Fisher's band. But I think of the three that I liked Shilling's group the best because they featured, when they'd go into that prize fight, they had all brass except your clarinet. It was, I mean, right on down the line, carnet, trombone, clarinet, tuba, French horn, and never a string bass and they had drums. That was it. And boy, they were hell-bent for election. I have one memory, Bill, which I someday am going to try to track down by going up to the fraternity house and it's so clear in my mind and I've had arguments with people because the date is so clear. I was being rushed as a freshman into several fraternities at Tulane and this party was being given at the Phi Delta Theater House. They had hired this white band which I still am under the impression it was Tom Brown's band and it was in the spring of the year because that's when rushing goes on for the season, you see. And they had hired the band from nine until one and everybody liked it so much that they wouldn't go home so the fraternity boys chipped in again and hired them from one until three and they liked them so well that the dancers all chipped in and they kept them until six and they were leaving that morning for Chicago and they left the fraternity house on State Street near Claiborne and walked in the street playing music and me in the crowd until they put them on the train. Now that's a memory that's too big and too many people. I can't get anybody in Tom Brown's band to remember that. Now the only thing that I would say would be that second group that followed Tom's band so closely. Was that Stein? Stein went up with
Yeah, it was pretty well mixed up to different personnel.
Yes, but who went up with Tom Brown's band first? Was it Wait?
Ray Lopez.
No, I mean the drummer.
Oh, the drummer.
Oh, shucks. No, it's no use wasting your tape.
I can't think of that. That's all right. Anyway.
But I can give it to you.
Anyway, we have I think that dope we have pretty well.
Anyway, it was the group. Larry Shields was not with Tom's outfit to start with. He was with them to start with. Then the second
Yellow Nunes came.
And then Gus Emala.
Gus Emala, that's right.
They swapped. Gus Emala for Larry Shields.
Shields went to the rocker then, yeah.

But it's one of those groups and I'm inclined to believe it's the second one since I know so many of them in the Brown Band. What year was that about? Can you remember? 1915. 1915, yeah. I'm pretty sure because that's the year I was going into Tulane. It would make me 18 years old then, you see?
Yeah, that's right.
But to me that's one of the most important memories that I have because
You wouldn't forget that.
Uh-uh. Now, I did not hear any of the white bands when I was in Chicago. The New Orleans Rhythm Kings were playing but somehow I missed them. I did hear all of them. How many years
were you in Chicago?

I was in Chicago from 1921 to 1925. And one interesting thing that I did hear and I was not aware of what I was hearing was Charlie Strait's band at the rendezvous which I got a job He was. He was. And I remember a small group when the big band would quit these five fellas would stay on the bandstand. And it would consist of tuba, piano, drums, cornet and I don't remember which other instrument. But I remember the music was a little disturbing to me. It was not in the either dance idiom like the band was playing straight or like the New Orleans idiom it was something brand new that was not appealing to me. Now, I think how ashamed I ought to be because I love Big so much now.
Probably some of his in the mist type of thing.

Exactly going on. Nobody was paying attention to him. It was a relief to get the band off and have a little quiet. We all used to bring our liquor and they'd furnish the setups for you. But that's one I heard three or four times up there and then I was fortunate enough to go to hear Oliver later on and I can't peg down in my mind just exactly which place it was except that I remember how it looked it was dirty and dingy and boy it smelled a beer the minute you walked in. On the second floor? No, it was on the first floor and you went through a long alleyway and made a turn.
It must have been the Royal Garden.
I think it was.
Huttage Grove in the second floor and I remember

at the time that Lillian Chris from New Orleans was my wife's best friend. She came up to spend some time with us and another intern by the name of Bill Ryan, Joe Ryan was her date and we went over there and we decided not to dance so the girls wouldn't be exposed to breaks because any of those places anybody could come up to you and ask for part of it. Well, many times these colored boys would even come up to your table even though your wife wasn't dancing and say, could I have part of this? We had instructed them carefully to be gentle in the way they spoke and nobody was offended and there was no humbug at all but it was rough.
Oh, that's the way in those days, yeah.
Now, I did hear Coon Sanders at the Black Hawk and I did hear Jimmy Noon a couple of times. Was that the Apex Club?
Yeah, the Nest that was called first of the Apex.
The Nest is what I knew it at the time and then another place that we used to go was a stable.
Oh, yeah. Up on the north.
Yeah.
Yeah, the side of the river.
Just over the Chicago Bridge there and that's about it as far as Chicago who I heard and all.
What did you call it? Graduate work or just getting your medical...

No, I went out first two years I finished in medicine in Chicago my junior and senior year. Then I went back for two years of internship. I came home got married and brought my wife right back. Then the way we celebrated my graduation not graduation my passing the state board by going to hear Joe Oliver. We didn't know who it was. Somebody in Chicago said, oh, we have the finest band you ever listened to up here. The nearer I got to it the more I knew it was Joe. I couldn't miss it,
you know.

But when we come back to the Owls they started out with a nucleus of about five, six men and they sometimes would go on up to six or eight. Now there's an overlap that's interesting here that I had no idea until I read a manuscript written by Marilyn Fletcher after interviews with Gussie Muller and Ray Lopez that, what the hell my trainer thought then about?
Oh, since it's interrupted what about the book that Gussie and Ray Lopez

has? I have tried to peddle it three or four places even overseas. They accepted it for the book The Month Club over in England and then they turned it down after sending me a wire that they accepted it so finally she asked me to take it back which I did but they're overlooking something because what they don't like about it is these guys are too humble. They claim they're not big men. They have not made a lot of records and we're not trained. We're just writing our story to show you how it fits into the picture and boy, they began with a hotbed of all the musicians that we know. Somebody will surely
bring that out, won't they?
I don't see how it can miss. I wish I had the money to publish it myself.
Of course it's a funny business a publishing business.

Oh here's what I started to tell you my train of thought. Mose Farrer F-E-R-R-E-R Farrer played piano with the Owls. When that piano player went up with them on a low account had a fallen out with Brown's band. They brought Mose Farrer up to play in Brown's band which I didn't know. It was a very short while but he did play with them in Chicago for about a month or six weeks. Mose was a pianist, his brother was a violinist and his mother was a professional music teacher. They lived sometime somewhere up around Napoleon Avenue a block or two above or below but towards Magazine Street.
Well I think of it do you have any information on Arnold Licano? Last time I saw Papa Lane it's been three or four months now maybe. He said that Arnold Licano was so sick.

Well he's not to the point of dying but he has had a very severe ulcer which I fooled around with for about three or four years and I finally got him in the hands of a good internist who's treating him and he's better.
Do you think he could be interviewed again? We have that interview you very kindly let us copy
That's a long damn thing that I have that I'll let you
have the whole business I don't think it was about three maybe an hour and a half three reels we may have all of it
I'm sure he'd be tickled to death Do you think
he would have any more information or do you think
his memory would be pretty bad now? Oh no I think he's just barely touched no he's clear as a bell clear as a bell
Would it be a hardship on him
his help? I think he would love it
You think he'd be alright?
Oh yes
I was afraid I'd start to keep
up on him No he's not that bad at all
As long as we had your interview I thought

we'd be happy with that No I think you could get more you know more about your audience than I do anyhow and you could ask him leading questions that would be very successful Now as I said that the owls they to me forsook the dance music that we were accustomed to dancing to and when they began being popular for the dances around New Orleans it was hard to dance to them their tempos were too fast and they had forsaken that easy going way you know but a very wonderful listening stuff and although they used music it was a bare outline their arrangements were intros and ride outs and maybe little duet breaks and things like that which were head arrangements and some of it was written arrangements but most of the time was all extemporaneous I think that Red Long I'm pretty sure he played with them for a while do you remember if I'm right on that trumpet
I'm not real sure I don't know what about the halfway house oh

brother they were terrific I remember the place out there was right at the corner of the what is now City Park Avenue and the New Basin Canal and the reputation of the place was that if anybody went in there they were forever damned to perdition and I finally raked up enough nerves to go in and it was the most innocuous place that you could go to during
prohibition times I guess it came up wasn't it

yes but it was clean but they had sawdust on the floor and they had sometimes sand on the floor you hear the dancers shuffling when they were dancing and I have a picture that I want to show you which is I'm going to use eventually in which I'll be glad to give you a copy after I've used it's the only interior shot I have ever seen well I got that and I remember the dance there only had four or five pieces and I didn't even know who the boys were then although what's his name Charlie Cardilla is a patient of mine and I've gotten a great deal of material from him both in pictures and in interviews and stuff and of course Brunies they had a fine band which not only played there they also had a brass band of sorts which they had within their own damn family as you know what's his name I think Arnold Lawyer Canada told me that I don't care what instrument you wanted you either could go up there and rent it for 50 cents a night up to a tube of any kind they had everything you wanted up there I didn't know those boys at that time because I was more or less sheltered in my own little old neighborhood
down in the Irish Channel a pretty tough place
whether out yeah that's about out too you got a little bit more
about another minute I hope I wouldn't have to
go
a little longer but if you have time I have
all the time you want it's up to you I don't want to bore you I
would like

to say something before this reel runs out about the style changes that I find today and in the old days I think that they are very correct in trying to preserve as you have done the traditional old musicians because they are the only ones that are playing actually the way it was done in the old days and I don't think they could vary because they wouldn't know how to vary now one thing that I do notice which follows a thought that I've always had is one of the reasons those men always sounded fresh and like they would

You mentioned the reason the men sound fresh today is, no I mean the reason they sounded fresh in the old days, because they weren't working regularly. They enjoyed playing this once a week or once every two weeks. In the old days they didn't work always steadily? No, no indeed they all had jobs and they got as much kick or more to get paid for doing something that they were crazy about doing. Now you take just these fellas now, these old timers that they've dug up and they're playing at Preservation Hall, they are losing that by the fact that they're playing regularly. And the people are hollering saints and all that crap at them and they are fed up to death with the thing and they're beginning to show it already. And another thing too, a band that starts playing together, they say to themselves, oh my god if that guy makes that same run or that same mistake I'm going to die and sure enough it's going to come out every time at the same place. And that's something that brings up another point that I made. There's some of those colored bands that have never solved a little bridge, I don't know how to describe it, but it goes into a minor sort of a key. They will play discord on that every time and never get over it and after 50 years they're going to do it the same mistakes every time. Are you aware? I mean I'm sure you've been aware of that. But their tone is different. What I particularly like is the dynamics of the Negro band. It's hell bent for election and everybody's having a hell of a good time. And no white drummers ever drum like a nigger except Jack. Jack did a beautiful job on those drums of his. And I think he was more Negro, although he disclaims any exposure at all to it. He couldn't help hear it. It was all over here.
Well he said he had some light colored fellows like Bach Kay and his band. And they passed for white. Yeah a few of those. Sure.

That's what Tom Brown was so ugly about. He said that old nigger he referred to Jack as a nigger. Because I'm sure he knew and Tom played with those boys too. There were two of them. Was it Rag Baby Steven?
Wasn't he? I don't know. I don't think I ever heard him say that.
Well now wait. That was Yellow Nunes.
Well that's the... Both Mama Lane and she said she knew the family. She said...

segments.title: Opening and Souchon's birth and family name
segments.summary: Russell opens the interview at Souchon's office on Feb 17, 1962. Souchon gives his birth date (Oct 25, 1897), his name as Edmond Souchon II, and says his grandfather delivered him.

segments.title: Earliest memories: sister's birth, the impaled horse
segments.summary: Souchon and Russell compare how far back they can remember. He recalls his sister's birth and the neighbours' stallion impaled on the picket fence.

segments.title: The cooks Amotin and Adele and their hymn singing
segments.summary: Two household cooks sang contralto hymns with bent, flattened notes, his earliest music memory. It was close to the style of Mahalia Jackson.

segments.title: Funeral parades and seeing young Joe Oliver
segments.summary: His cook took him to second-line funeral parades from the Washington Avenue cemetery. There he was drawn to the young cornetist Joe Oliver, who worked as a yard man. Russell adds where Oliver lived.

segments.title: Joe Oliver's white teeth and chewing tar
segments.summary: A childhood impression of Oliver as a teenager with beautiful white teeth who always chewed a lump of tar.

segments.title: Music in the family home and grandfather's records
segments.summary: His mother played piano a little and his father played French horn and guitar in college. His grandfather's house had a player piano, ragtime records, cylinder phonographs and a music box.

segments.title: Guitar lessons, dancing school trio and Armand's Pass Christian band
segments.summary: A grandmother, an aunt's ukulele and three failed classical guitar lessons come first. Ragtime players at a neighbour's dancing school then draw him back to the guitar. He takes cheap lessons from the chauffeur-bandleader Armand and hears Buddy Petit's band compete with him.

segments.title: Buddy Petit's swelling neck and other players' cheeks
segments.summary: Souchon describes how Buddy Petit's neck and face puffed out when he blew. Russell compares Armstrong, Brunies and Jim Robinson.

segments.title: Pass Christian wharf spasm band and the local saxophone band
segments.summary: A four-piece homemade string band of boys played for two dollars, including the song Yonder Come the Hoodoo Conducta Man. Souchon confirms the larger band was all local and says its saxophones made it sound different from New Orleans bands.

segments.title: The Reynolds brothers' Sunday string group
segments.summary: At about eleven he joins Bob and Harry Reynolds' Sunday sessions on Britannia Street. He lists the group: violinists Hilton Harrison and Rex, Bernie Shields on banjo, Charlie Hardy on ukulele and Bill Gibbons.

segments.title: Going out to parties, meeting his wife, and the rival Invincibles
segments.summary: After three years of practice, at about fourteen the group begins playing at girls' houses, where he meets his future wife. The better string group, the Invincibles, becomes the Owls.

segments.title: Staying close to Johnny St. Cyr; his cataract and guitar
segments.summary: He had no formal lessons but stayed beside Johnny St. Cyr at the Tulane gym dances, and they are still friends. They discuss St. Cyr's wife's death, his cataract operation and the guitar he plans to send the museum.

segments.title: Mardi Gras parades passing his house
segments.summary: As a child of six or seven he saw Mardi Gras parades with one jazz band, Jack Laine's, stopping before his house. People danced in the street and the militia met the king.

segments.title: Fraternity and gym dance bands: McCollum, Armstrong, riverboat bands
segments.summary: Gym dances cost a dollar a couple. For fraternity dances they hired McCollum's cheap band and sometimes Armstrong's loud band. The dance bands he lists include the Silver Leaf and Tuxedo.

segments.title: Robichaux's band at La Louisiane
segments.summary: Robichaux was a polished left-handed violinist whose house band at La Louisiane played from arrangements. He hired hot players such as Perez and Lorenzo Tio Jr., and waltzes came every third or fourth dance.

segments.title: Dance steps then and now: two-step, one-step, the Castles
segments.summary: He describes intricate close-contact two-step and one-step dancing, Irene Castle dancing to Piron's band at the St. Charles, and how dancing differs today.

segments.title: Oliver's band at the Tulane dances: pay, whiskey, the singing drummer
segments.summary: A dance cost a dollar. The Oliver band got $28 for seven men plus whiskey, grew bluer as the evening wore on, and their drummer sang dirty songs.

segments.title: Oliver at his peak and the slow march tempo of High Society
segments.summary: Oliver's playing polished up from the rough Big 25 days. High Society was originally a slow, dirge-like supper march, not a dance tune. Russell says Black dances used Gettysburg and the 6-8 in the same way.

segments.title: Oliver's sidemen, sustained notes, Chicago change, and diabetes
segments.summary: Souchon names sidemen and says no record shows Oliver's single sustained note. In Chicago Oliver had changed his style and added saxes. Ory's West Coast group came closest to the old sound. Souchon suspects Oliver had diabetes.

segments.title: Oliver's cut shoes, red undershirt and the nickname Monocle
segments.summary: Oliver slit his new shoes to ease his feet and wore a red undershirt and a derby. He was affectionately called Monocle because of the white eye that bulged when he played.

segments.chapter: Guitarists and the Pierron and Brown bands
segments.title: Guitar versus banjo in early bands; St. Cyr's capo and pick
segments.summary: Few banjos were in the early bands. Johnny St. Cyr played a homemade six-string guitar with a pencil capo and a toothbrush pick. Players used thumb and index finger, and Souchon's three classical lessons ruined his playing.

segments.chapter: Guitarists and the Pierron and Brown bands
segments.title: Thompson McKay and Snoozer Quinn, the greatest guitarist
segments.summary: Thompson McKay played plantation-style guitar. Snoozer Quinn is called the best guitarist ever, with vibrato, a violin stunt, and a stint with the Owls at Suburban Gardens.

segments.chapter: Guitarists and the Pierron and Brown bands
segments.title: Piron's band: Lorenzo Tio, Cottrell and the banjoists
segments.summary: Piron's band read arrangements but took hot breaks, led by Lorenzo Tio. Souchon corrects an earlier statement about Steve Lewis and recalls drummer Cottrell's moving eyebrows. He and Russell try to name the banjoist.

segments.chapter: Guitarists and the Pierron and Brown bands
segments.title: Tuba versus string bass; Chink Martin
segments.summary: Piron's band featured the tuba while Oliver's used string bass, probably for slap rhythm without a piano. Chink Martin carries tuba and bass on the street at 74.

segments.chapter: Guitarists and the Pierron and Brown bands
segments.title: Why Souchon prefers banjo to guitar in a band
segments.summary: He would rather play banjo with a band because it kicks the rhythm along and cannot be turned off the microphone. The old guitar could be heard only near the band.

segments.chapter: Guitarists and the Pierron and Brown bands
segments.title: Happy Schilling's, Brown's and Fisher's bands; the all-night Brown party
segments.summary: He liked Schilling's all-brass prize-fight band best. He recalls a Phi Delta Theta rush party where a white band, probably Tom Brown's, played until dawn and marched to the Chicago train.

segments.chapter: Guitarists and the Pierron and Brown bands
segments.title: Sorting out Brown's band personnel; dating the memory to 1915
segments.summary: Souchon and Russell try to recall the band's drummers and the Shields-for-Emala swap. Souchon dates the memory to 1915, the year he entered Tulane.

segments.title: Chicago 1921-25: missing the Rhythm Kings; Charlie Straight's band
segments.summary: Souchon was in Chicago from 1921 to 1925 and missed the New Orleans Rhythm Kings. He heard Charlie Straight's band at the Rendezvous and disliked the small group's new music, which he now regrets.

segments.title: Hearing Oliver at the Royal Garden with his wife and friends
segments.summary: He recalls a dingy, beery club, probably the Royal Garden, where Black musicians would ask to share a customer's table. His party instructed them to be gentle.

segments.title: Other Chicago bands and clubs: Coon-Sanders, Noone, the Nest
segments.summary: He lists the Chicago acts he heard, Coon-Sanders at the Black Hawk, Jimmie Noone at the Apex/Nest and a stable on the north side.

segments.title: Finishing medical training and celebrating by hearing Oliver
segments.summary: He finished medicine in Chicago, did two years of internship, married and returned. He celebrated passing the state board by following the sound to Joe Oliver's band.

segments.chapter: The Owls and New Orleans after the war
segments.title: The Owls, Fletcher's manuscript, and Mose Ferrer in Brown's band
segments.summary: He describes the Owls' early lineup and the unpublished manuscript by Marilyn Fletcher. The pianist Mose Ferrer, his brother and his mother are discussed, and Ferrer played briefly with Brown's band in Chicago.

segments.chapter: The Owls and New Orleans after the war
segments.title: Arnold Loyacano's illness and a possible new interview
segments.summary: Souchon says Loyacano had a severe ulcer, now treated by an internist. They agree he is mentally sharp and could be interviewed again.

segments.chapter: The Owls and New Orleans after the war
segments.title: The Owls' fast tempos and head arrangements
segments.summary: The Owls were hard to dance to because of fast tempos but wonderful to listen to, using mostly head arrangements. Souchon thinks Red Long played with them.

segments.chapter: The Owls and New Orleans after the war
segments.title: The Halfway House and the Brunies family band
segments.summary: The Halfway House at City Park Avenue and the New Basin Canal was reputed to be wicked but was innocuous, with sawdust floors. The Brunies family also rented out instruments.

segments.chapter: The Owls and New Orleans after the war
segments.title: Reel running out; Souchon says he has time
segments.summary: They discuss the reel nearly running out, and Souchon says he has all the time Russell wants.

segments.title: Why old-time bands sounded fresh; Preservation Hall and Black band dynamics
segments.summary: Old bands sounded fresh because they played only occasionally. Preservation Hall musicians are losing it by playing nightly. Souchon prizes the dynamics of Black bands and says Jack Laine drummed like a Black drummer.

segments.title: Jack Laine's band and light-skinned musicians passing as white
segments.summary: Russell says some light-skinned musicians passed for white. Souchon recalls Tom Brown's slur against Laine and wonders about others, including Yellow Nunez.
